predecessors.note: The Later Jin page lists as predecessors 'Jianzhou Jurchens, Ming dynasty, Northern Yuan'. The Jianzhou Jurchens were a tribal confederation with no Cliopatria row, so the Ming, their nominal suzerain, stands as the slug; the Nurhaci page dates the subduing of the core Jianzhou tribes to 1583-1588, Hada 1603, Hoifa 1607 and an Ula expedition in 1613.

land.text: the whole Later Jin / Qing realm of 1642-1644, from which the Qing row of Cliopatria begins in 1645

successors.note: The same state: Hong Taiji renamed the realm Great Qing in 1636 (rename event). Cliopatria keeps the name 'Later Jin Dynasty' for 1636-1644 and starts its 'Qing Dynasty' row in 1645, which is why this dossier ends in 1644. The Qing dossier (qing-dynasty, group ea-08-b) should take over the colour; it must restart the Joseon tributary relation (vassal_start 1637 here) and the Liaoxi / Shanhai corridor.

capitals.note: Nurhaci page: 'In April 1625, he designated Shenyang the new capital city, which would hold that status until the Qing conquest of the Ming in 1644.' The Later Jin infobox gives Mukden 1625-1636; coordinates are the gazetteer's Shenyang.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria starts the Later Jin in 1619 but Nurhaci declared himself Khan and founded the Jin in 1616 (reign from 17 February 1616). The page dates the Hulun conquests (Hada 1603, Hoifa 1607, an Ula expedition in 1613) and names Hetu Ala as the first capital, but gives no boundary, so the shape is the researcher's reading: a radius round Hetu Ala and one round Jilin (the Ula country). Heilongjiang north of the Songhua is drawn whole from 1636 although the Hong Taiji page has the Amur expeditions run 1636-1644 and the Evenk conquest completed in 1640; kept, as a low-confidence ledger gain. union.text: Hetu Ala, the Jin capital 1616-1622 (coordinate approximate; the gazetteer lacks the name)
the Ula country on the Songhua and the neighbouring Hulun tribes (Hoifa, Hada), subdued 1603-1613

region.text: the Jianzhou Jurchen core round Hetu Ala and the Hulun tribes subdued by 1613

ledger.note: 1616: Nurhaci declares himself Khan and founds the Jin (the Later Jin) at Hetu Ala. 'In 1616, Nurhaci declared himself Khan and founded the Jin dynasty (aisin gurun)'; 'Reign: 17 February 1616 - 30 September 1626'. The page gives the year and the tribes he had subdued (Jianzhou core 1583-1588, Hada 1603, Hoifa 1607, Ula 1613), not a boundary, so the region is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Liaodong: Liaoyang, Shenyang and the peninsula

ledger.note: 1618: Nurhaci issues the Seven Grievances against the Ming and attacks in Liaodong. 'In 1618, Nurhaci commissioned a document titled the Seven Grievances'; the Later Jin page adds that he 'occupied Fushun and Qinghe before retreating'. The Liaodong campaign runs 1618-1621; the zone is the researcher's reading of the towns named.

region.text: Fushun, surrendered in 1618

ledger.note: 1618: Fushun passes to the Jin. Li Yongfang 'surrendered Fushun in Liaoning to the Manchus in 1618'. The Later Jin page says Nurhaci 'occupied Fushun and Qinghe before retreating', so the first hold may have been brief.

region.text: Tieling, subdued in the summer of 1619

ledger.note: 1619: Tieling falls to Nurhaci. 'Nurhaci continues his campaign subduing Tieling in the summer of 1619.' Kaiyuan appears in the same narrative without a date.

region.text: the Yehe country, the last Hulun tribe, attacked in 1619

ledger.note: 1619: the Yehe, the last of the four Hulun tribes, are defeated. The Nurhaci page dates the Hulun campaign 1599-1618 and puts 'the Yehe and its beile Gintaisi' at 'the Battle of Sarhu in 1619'; the Later Jin page says 'In 1619, he attacked the Yehe in an attempt to provoke the Ming'. The page gives the tribe, not the land: the Siping area is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Liaodong: Liaoyang, Shenyang and the peninsula

ledger.note: May 1621: the Liaodong fighting ends in a Jin victory. 'By May 1621, Nurhaci had conquered the cities of Liaoyang and Shenyang.' The page gives 'by May', so month 5 is a bound.

region.text: the cities of Liaoyang and Shenyang

ledger.note: May 1621: Liaoyang and Shenyang pass to the Jin. 'By May 1621, Nurhaci had conquered the cities of Liaoyang and Shenyang.' Cliopatria's Ming and Later Jin shapes both change a year later, in 1622.

minus.text: Liaodong: Liaoyang, Shenyang and the peninsula

region.text: the rest of Liaodong, down the peninsula

ledger.note: 1622: the rest of Liaodong (the peninsula) is Jin land in Cliopatria's 1622 shape. The Nurhaci page is silent on these towns; its only 1622 sentence is 'In 1622, Nurhaci managed to defeat the Ming forces and killed 16,000 of their soldiers at the battle of Guangning'. Confidence 1: a date taken from the Cliopatria shapes (the Ming row also loses most of Liaodong in 1622).
1622: the court moves from Hetu Ala to Tungking (Liaoyang). Infobox 'Hetu Ala (1616-1622); Tungking (1622-1625); Mukden (1625-1636)'. The Tungking = Liaoyang identification is the researcher's.

April 1625: Shenyang becomes the capital. 'In April 1625, he designated Shenyang the new capital city, which would hold that status until the Qing conquest of the Ming in 1644.' The Later Jin infobox calls it Mukden.

region.text: north-western Korea across the frozen Yalu

ledger.note: February 1627: the Jin cross the frozen Yalu and invade Joseon. 'February 1627 his forces crossed the Yalu River which had frozen.' The joseon dossier (jk-02) dates the first advance 14 January 1627 from its own page; the zone (north-western Korea) is the researcher's reading of the Yalu crossing.

region.text: north-western Korea across the frozen Yalu

ledger.note: 1627: the Jin leave Korea. The invasion page says only that the 1636 war 'was preceded by the Later Jin invasion of Joseon in 1627' and gives no end date or terms; the joseon dossier (jk-02) dates the withdrawal 3 March 1627 from its own page. Confidence 1: the end, and the month 3 that keeps the ledger in order, are bridged from the joseon dossier, not read from this page.

region.text: the Chahar Mongol country under Ligden Khan

ledger.note: 1632: Hong Taiji and his Mongol allies march on Ligden Khan's Chahar. 'In 1632, the Later Jin khan Hong Taiji and his Mongol allies undertook a campaign against Ligden'; Ligden avoided battle and fled 'with perhaps 100,000 Chakhar to Kokenuur (Qinghai)'. Chahar's land is Inner Mongolia in the researcher's reading; the mongol-khanate dossier (ia-02) carries the same start.

region.text: the Chahar Mongol country under Ligden Khan

ledger.note: 1635: the Northern Yuan submit and the Chahar war ends. 'In 1635, the lingering Northern Yuan dynasty under Ejei Khan formally submitted to the Later Jin.' The Ligdan Khan page has Ligden dying of smallpox at Sira Tala in 1634 and Ejei Khan 'handed over to the Qing dynasty'. No month on either page; the mongol-khanate dossier (ia-02) dates the surrender February 1635 from its own page.

region.text: Inner Mongolia, the lands of Ligden's Chahar and the Mongol allies

ledger.note: 1635: Inner Mongolia passes to the Jin. Ejei Khan 'formally submitted to the Later Jin'; 'The Mongol allies were also incorporated into a separate Banner hierarchy that year.' The Hong Taiji page: he 'took over Inner Mongolia ... in three major wars' and set up the Mongol Yamen in 1636 for its indirect government. The year is the page's; the land is the researcher's reading. Cliopatria draws Inner Mongolia from 1636.

1636: Hong Taiji renames the realm Great Qing (the Later Jin ends in name, not in state). 'The following year, Hong Taiji officially renamed the realm to "Great Qing."' The Kurultai at Shenyang that recommended it met in April 1636; the Hong Taiji page has him changing the era name to Chongde in 1636, and the name 'Manchu' had been adopted in November 1635.

region.text: Heilongjiang as Cliopatria's 1636 shape draws it

ledger.note: 1636: Cliopatria draws all of Heilongjiang as Jin land from 1636. The Hong Taiji page has only 'From 1636 until 1644, he sent 4 major expeditions into the Amur region' and the Evenk conquest completed in 1640; it dates no earlier conquest of the Songhua-Nen country. Confidence 1: the date and land come from the Cliopatria shape.

region.text: the Amur region

ledger.counterpart: Evenk and Daur tribes of the Amur
ledger.note: 1636: the first Amur expedition. 'From 1636 until 1644, he sent 4 major expeditions into the Amur region.' The peoples were tribes (Evenks, Daurs); the Amur basin as a zone is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the three-pronged advance from the Yalu to the Han valley and Ganghwa

ledger.note: 9 December 1636: Hong Taiji invades Joseon. 'On 9 December 1636, Hong Taiji led Manchu, Mongol, and Han Chinese Banners in a three pronged attack on Joseon.' Joseon 'did not recognize Hong Taiji's newly declared dynasty'. The zone is the researcher's reading: the route from the Yalu to the Han valley and Ganghwa Island. Confidence 2: the date is the page's, the zone (all of North Korea plus Gyeonggi) is the researcher's reading (reviewer ea-08-a, 2026-10-24).

region.text: the three-pronged advance from the Yalu to the Han valley and Ganghwa

ledger.note: 28 January 1637: King Injo surrenders. 'Dorgon occupied Ganghwa Island on 27 January, and captured the second son and consorts of King Injo. King Injo surrendered the day after.' The surrender was made at Samjeondo on the upper Han. Confidence 2: the date is the page's, the zone (all of North Korea plus Gyeonggi) is the researcher's reading (reviewer ea-08-a, 2026-10-24).

region.text: the whole kingdom of Joseon, as Cliopatria draws it once the northern strip returns in 1640

ledger.note: January 1637: Joseon becomes a Qing tributary. 'Joseon was forced to establish a tributary relationship with the Qing'; terms: drop the Ming name and seals, send two princes as hostages, accept the Qing calendar, supply troops, build no fortresses, send tribute every year. Infobox 'Joseon switches tributary allegiance from the Ming to the Qing.' No territory changes hands. The relation outlasts this dossier (no vassal_end): the Qing dossier should restart it in 1645.

region.text: western Liaoning: the Guangning-Jinzhou-Songshan side of the Liao River

ledger.note: 1640: the battles for Songshan and Jinzhou begin. The Later Jin page dates 'a series of battles for Songshan and Jinzhou' 'from 1640 to 1642'. The page does not give the result.

region.text: the Amur region

ledger.counterpart: Evenk and Daur tribes of the Amur
ledger.note: 1640: the Evenks are conquered. 'In 1640 he completed the conquest of the Evenks, when he defeated and captured their leader Bombogor.' The Amur expeditions continue to 1644.

region.text: the Amur region of the Evenks and Daurs

ledger.note: 1640: the Amur region passes to the Jin. The Evenk conquest is complete in 1640 (Bombogor captured) after expeditions from 1636. The page names the Amur region, not its extent: Cliopatria's 1640 shape adds 2,689 cells of Outer Manchuria and the region name is the researcher's reading.

region.text: western Liaoning: the Guangning-Jinzhou-Songshan side of the Liao River

ledger.note: 1642: the battles for Songshan and Jinzhou end. 'A series of battles for Songshan and Jinzhou, dated from 1640 to 1642.'

region.text: western Liaoning: the Guangning-Jinzhou-Songshan side of the Liao River

ledger.note: 1642: Liaoxi (Jinzhou, Songshan) is Jin land in Cliopatria's 1642 shape. The Later Jin page: Hong Taiji was able 'to resoundingly defeat Ming forces in a series of battles from 1640 to 1642 for the territories of Songshan and Jinzhou'; the Hong Taiji page has the Qing still 'preparing to attack Shanhai Pass' in September 1643. Confidence 2: the page names Songshan and Jinzhou, not the whole of Liaoxi; whether Ningyuan and the corridor to the Shanhai Pass fell before 1644 is not on the page. Liaoxi is limited to the side west of the Liao River (the gazetteer's Liaoxi also holds Kaiyuan and northern Liaoning, Jin since 1619). Reviewer ea-08-a, 2026-10-24.

region.text: the whole realm of 1642-1644, continuing as the Qing

ledger.note: 1644: Cliopatria's 'Later Jin Dynasty' row ends and its 'Qing Dynasty' row begins in 1645. The state does not end: the Nurhaci page has Shenyang the capital 'until the Qing conquest of the Ming in 1644' and the Later Jin page has Li Zicheng's Shun forces taking Beijing in 1644 and the Qing defeating them later. Confidence 1: the year is Cliopatria's row boundary; the land passes to the same state under its Qing name (qing-dynasty).

wars.name: Nurhaci's conquest of Liaodong (Seven Grievances to Guangning)

zones.text: Fushun and Tieling (1618-1619), Liaoyang and Shenyang (by May 1621), Guangning (1622)

wars.outcome: Jin victory: Fushun 1618, Tieling 1619, Liaoyang and Shenyang by May 1621, the Ming defeated at Guangning in 1622 with 16,000 killed. A Joseon force under General Gang Hong-rip, sent in 1619, later surrendered at Sarhu.
wars.note: The Later Jin page: 1618 Seven Grievances, 'Fushun and Qinghe' occupied; 1619 attack on the Yehe and 'the Battle of Sarhu' that winter. The Nurhaci page does not date Sarhu, Kaiyuan or Qinghe.

wars.name: Ningyuan and the Yuan Chonghuan defences
wars.outcome: Ming defensive victories: Nurhaci was defeated at Ningyuan in January 1626, the Jurchens again in 1627, and Hong Taiji in 1628, all by Yuan Chonghuan; no border moved.
wars.note: 'The unbroken series of military successes by Nurhaci came to an end in January 1626.' The Hong Taiji page has the 1628 defeat 'and his use of artillery'. Neither page names the places of the 1627 and 1628 battles.

wars.name: Later Jin invasion of Joseon (1627)

zones.text: north-western Korea across the frozen Yalu

wars.outcome: The Jin crossed the Yalu in February 1627 and left; the terms are not on the pages opened.
wars.note: The invasion page says only that the 1636 invasion 'was preceded by the Later Jin invasion of Joseon in 1627'.

wars.name: Chahar campaigns against Ligden Khan

zones.text: the Chahar Mongol country under Ligden Khan

wars.outcome: Ligden fled in 1632 with perhaps 100,000 Chahar to Kokenuur (Qinghai), died of smallpox at Sira Tala in 1634 and his son Ejei Khan submitted to the Later Jin in 1635; Inner Mongolia passed to the Jin.
wars.note: The Eastern Tumens deserted to Nurhaci in 1622-24 and the Khorchin 'bonded with the Manchus in 1624' (Ligdan Khan page): alliances, not territory. 'Hong Taiji took over Inner Mongolia ... in three major wars' (Hong Taiji page, no years).

wars.name: Jin raids into Ming territory (Shanxi raids of 1632 and 1634)
wars.outcome: Raids took no ground. 'First attack went through the Jehol Pass, then in 1632 and 1634 he sent raids into Shanxi.'
wars.note: The Jehol Pass raid is undated on the page.

wars.name: Qing invasion of Joseon

zones.text: the three-pronged advance from the Yalu to the Han valley and Ganghwa

wars.outcome: Qing victory: Injo surrendered on 28 January 1637 and Joseon became a Qing tributary, breaking with the Ming; no cession of land.
wars.note: Began 9 December 1636; Dorgon took Ganghwa Island on 27 January 1637. The page does not use the name 'Treaty of Samjeondo'.

wars.name: Amur expeditions and the conquest of the Evenks
belligerents: Evenk and Daur tribes of the Amur
wars.outcome: Four major expeditions between 1636 and 1644; the Evenk conquest was completed in 1640 with the capture of Bombogor.
wars.note: The page names the Evenks and the Amur region; the Daurs and the extent of the zone are the researcher's reading.

wars.name: Battles for Songshan and Jinzhou

zones.text: western Liaoning: the Guangning-Jinzhou-Songshan side of the Liao River

wars.outcome: Jin (Qing) victory: the Later Jin page has Hong Taiji 'resoundingly' defeating the Ming 'in a series of battles from 1640 to 1642 for the territories of Songshan and Jinzhou'; Cliopatria draws Liaoxi as Qing land from 1642.
wars.note: Hong Taiji died on 21 September 1643 'just as the Qing was preparing to attack Shanhai Pass' (Hong Taiji page).

certainty.note: No treaty line or survey bounds the Jin: the Ming frontier in Liaodong and Liaoxi moves with sieges, the Mongol and Amur frontiers are tribal and approximate. The Joseon relation of 1637 is a tributary tie, not a border treaty.

notes: Written by ea-08-a on 2026-10-24 from five pages (the budget for eight shapes) fetched through WebFetch, whose extracts are quoted; none carries an area, so no keyframe could be compared with an infobox. 1. One state, two Cliopatria rows: Wikipedia's Later Jin page ends in 1636 with the renaming to Great Qing, and the Qing dynasty page starts in 1636, but Cliopatria keeps the name 'Later Jin Dynasty' to 1644 (8 shapes, 1619-1644) and starts 'Qing Dynasty' in 1645 (61 shapes). This dossier follows the Cliopatria rows (start 1616, rename 1636, end 1644); the colour agent should give later-jin-dynasty and qing-dynasty the same family and ideally the same colour (rule 2), or the orchestrator may merge them under qing-dynasty. 2. Cliopatria faults found and corrected (see keyframe_review): the 1619 shape lies in eastern Jilin and omits the capital Hetu Ala, Fushun and Tieling; the 1622 shape stops short of Shenyang and Liaoyang although the Nurhaci page has both conquered by May 1621; the 1626-1628 shape holds Liaoxi (Jinzhou) in the year Nurhaci lost at Ningyuan; the Hulun plains of central Jilin (Ula 1613, Yehe 1619) are drawn only from 1632; the 1636-1639 shape takes 162 cells of Korea (135 in North Korea, 27 round Seoul) although Joseon only became a tributary; Liaoxi is drawn as Jin land in 1636-1641 although the battles for Songshan and Jinzhou are dated 1640-1642.
